hints: Start by sorting what you see in Fig. 1.1 - dark stacked membranes, the thin membrane joining them, the fluid background, and the tiny dark dots in the fluid.
Remember the big split in photosynthesis - the membranes that trap light versus the fluid where carbon dioxide is fixed into sugar.
For protons, think of a pump in a membrane and a closed space inside where protons can be stored at high concentration.
For proteins, look for the tiny structures in the fluid background that are built for translation, just like in bacteria.
walkthrough:
Read the micrograph like a map**
A is the pale fluid background, so that is the stroma. B is the dark stacked discs, so that is the granum made of thylakoids and the space inside them is the thylakoid lumen. C is the membrane itself forming the thylakoid. D is a tiny dot free in the stroma, so that is a chloroplast ribosome.

Match function to structure**
Light energy drives proton pumps in the thylakoid membrane, so C pumps protons. The pumped protons collect inside the sealed lumen, so B accumulates a high concentration of protons for chemiosmosis through ATP synthase. The Calvin cycle fixes carbon dioxide into triose phosphate using ATP and reduced NADP, and those enzymes are in the stroma, so A makes triose phosphate. Chloroplasts have their own small 70S ribosomes for making some of their own proteins, so D makes some chloroplast proteins.

Final answer: accumulates high concentration of protons - B (thylakoid lumen in granum); makes triose phosphate - A (stroma); makes some chloroplast proteins - D (chloroplast ribosome); pumps protons - C (thylakoid membrane).

hints: Think how to put the liquid extract onto chromatography paper so all pigments start from exactly the same narrow starting line.
Think about the solvent level in the tank - where must it be relative to your starting spot so pigments are carried and not washed off.
Think what you need to mark and measure once the coloured spots have separated and stopped moving.
Think how a simple ratio of two distances lets you identify each pigment by comparing with known values.
walkthrough:
Set up a clean start**
Draw a pencil baseline near the bottom of the paper - pencil because ink would dissolve and add extra pigments. Place a small spot of the extract of membrane C on the line, let it dry, then spot again on top to concentrate the pigments into a small intense spot.

Run the chromatogram**
Stand the paper upright in a covered tank with a suitable solvent, with the solvent level below the baseline so the spot is not submerged. The solvent rises by capillarity and carries the different pigments at different rates according to their solubility in the solvent and attraction to the paper.

Measure and identify**
Before the solvent reaches the top, remove the paper and immediately mark the solvent front in pencil. When dry, measure for each spot: $R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by pigment from baseline}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front from baseline}}$. Compare each $R_f$ and colour with known $R_f$ values for chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, xanthophyll and carotene to identify the yellow, orange, green-brown and green pigments.

Final answer: Place a spot of extract on the pencil baseline / origin line and concentrate by re-spotting and drying; suspend paper with base in solvent below the baseline; allow solvent to rise, then mark solvent front; calculate $R_f$ = distance moved by pigment / distance moved by solvent front and compare with known $R_f$ values to identify pigments.

hints: Think what a different colour actually means - which wavelengths of light are reflected and which are absorbed.
Think what would be wasted if the thylakoid had only one type of chlorophyll that absorbs only red and blue light well.
Think how passing extra captured energy to the reaction centre changes the rate of the light-dependent reaction.
walkthrough:
Different colours mean different light captured**
Membrane C is the thylakoid membrane where light harvesting happens. Chlorophyll a absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green. Accessory pigments such as chlorophyll b, carotene (orange) and xanthophyll (yellow) absorb other wavelengths, for example green-yellow and green-brown regions, that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly.

More wavelengths means more energy for photosynthesis**
Energy absorbed by accessory pigments is passed to the reaction centre chlorophyll a. Together they broaden the action spectrum, so more of the white light spectrum is used. That supplies more ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent reaction, increasing the efficiency and rate of photosynthesis.

Final answer: Different pigments absorb / harvest different wavelengths of light; increases range of light that can be absorbed; increases rate / efficiency of photosynthesis / light-dependent reaction. e.g. chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotene, xanthophyll.
